query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A brief, rapid high-temperature annealing treatment applied post-synthesis to nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 redistributes Cr and V to the grain boundaries, thereby reducing their intragranular supersaturation and suppressing radiation-induced Cr/V precipitation under fusion-relevant energetic-particle irradiation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 produced with a uniform solid-solution distribution of W, Ta, Cr, and V.
generation.intervention: A short-duration high-temperature (e.g., >1050 K) anneal applied after fabrication.
generation.conditions: Exposure to energetic-particle irradiation up to ~8 dpa at temperatures around 1050 K, simulating fusion service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Induced pre-segregation of Cr and V to grain boundaries, which reduces their local concentration in the grain interior.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced atomic mobility during the anneal drives Cr and V solutes to segregate to grain boundaries, lowering the driving force for intragranular Cr/V rich precipitate formation during subsequent irradiation. This redistribution also maintains high defect recombination rates that help preserve low irradiation hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified alloy that forms 3–5 nm Cr/V-rich precipitates (≈0.03 nm⁻² density) after ~8 dpa, the annealed material will exhibit a significant reduction in precipitate formation (directional reduction, potentially >30% lower density) while retaining negligible irradiation hardening and offering improved microstructural stability for bulk fabrication.
generation.baseline: The unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy, which under identical irradiation conditions develops measurable intragranular Cr/V-rich precipitates and is prone to difficulties in bulk processing.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under fusion-relevant irradiation conditions (≈8 dpa) at elevated temperatures (≈1050 K). Thermal stability of the induced segregation should persist up to these service temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in precipitate density and the optimal annealing parameters (temperature and time) require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 samples: one set receives the rapid high-temperature annealing treatment and the other is left unmodified. Expose both sets to energetic-particle irradiation up to ~8 dpa at ~1050 K. Post-irradiation, characterize the precipitate density, size, and distribution (via TEM and atom probe tomography) and measure mechanical properties (e.g., hardness via nanoindentation).
measurements: TEM imaging to quantify precipitate size and density
Atom probe tomography (APT) for chemical segregation analysis
Grain boundary characterization to verify Cr/V segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >30% lower density) in intragranular Cr/V-rich precipitates and do not maintain or improve the irradiation hardening behavior relative to the unmodified control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The total change in volume was ~0.65% (from grain matrices only). The current alloy presents no loop formation and the total change in volume is ~0.3 % after 8.45 dpa and higher percentage of implanted He. Additionally, no preferential large and facetted cavity formation at the grain boundaries was observed. Irradiation with helium ions led to lattice shrinking in Ni and lattice expansion in NiCoFeCr and NiCoFeCrMn. The increase in the lattice parameter can be caused by the microstrain and defects generated by helium irradiation [], where point defects and small defect clusters increase the strain and lattice parameter, while larger clusters, such as dislocation loops, can reduce them []. The lattice expansion and microstrain decrease at higher irradiation temperatures, since it stimulates defect recombination, reduces the residual stress and lattice distortion, and the expansion depends not only on the irradiation conditions, but also on the constituent elements of the target [,]. The addition of Fe and Mn reduce the volume swelling in the Ni alloys []. The integrated experimental and modelling work shows that reduced defect mobility and altered migration paths on a modified energy landscape, resulting from alloy complexity, can modify defect dynamics to promote annihilation of radiation damage that ultimately enhance radiation tolerance. Irradiation-induced void formation in nickel and Ni-containing equiatomic SP-CSAs at elevated temperature is controlled by the migration behaviours of interstitial clusters. Short-range 3D motion of interstitial clusters that significantly increases the vacancy–interstitial recombination rate plays a key role in preventing significant void swelling in NiFe, NiCoFe, NiCoFeCr and NiCoFeCrMn. The mechanism has been revealed by TEM observation and confirmed by MD simulation. Composition complexity and lattice distortion due to the alloy components effectively modify the defect migration behaviour in the equiatomic SP-CSAs. More localized migration of interstitial clusters enhances recombination of point defects in the cascade region where the defects are created. cited_evidence.kind: web:Origin of Cr- and V-rich precipitates in the HEAs
cited_evidence.text: To understand the origin of the Cr- and V-rich precipitates observed in annealed and irradiated HEA samples, we have systematically carried out first-principles calculations of phase stability and chemical short-range order (SRO) of the multicomponent 38 at % W/36 at % Ta/15 at % Cr/11 at % V alloy as a function of temperature. The cluster expansion (CE) methodology [see Methods and refs. ()] has been used to build up an ab initio–based Hamiltonian with many-body effective cluster interactions (ECIs), from which the configurational entropy and therefore the free energy of multicomponent system can be obtained from thermodynamic integration techniques () in combination with canonical Monte Carlo (CMC) simulations. The enthalpies of mixing were calculated using the density functional theory (DFT) and CE methods for nearly 270 structures within the BCC underlying crystalline lattice. Values for all binary structures in the database were analyzed to determine the nature of the atomic interactions in all possible binary configurations (fig. S7). The positive and negative enthalpies of mixing values indicate a tendency for segregation or ordering, respectively.
